Pregnancy

Vomiting blood during pregnancy: when to get help

Updated: October 6, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Blood in vomit needs prompt medical assessment during pregnancy, even when you have been vomiting frequently or only notice a streak. It may be red, brown, black or resemble coffee grounds. Pregnancy sickness is common, but bleeding is not something to accept as part of it. Some causes are relatively minor; others need immediate hospital treatment. Appearance alone cannot tell you which applies.

Get help now rather than waiting for the next appointment

Seek emergency care for ongoing or substantial bleeding, or blood in vomit together with feeling unwell, dizziness, faintness, confusion, rapid breathing, cold clammy skin, abdominal pain or black tarry stools. Severe chest pain or difficulty breathing after retching is also an emergency. Do not drive yourself; use emergency services or have someone arrange safe transport.

If the bleeding has stopped and you have no other symptoms, contact your maternity team or urgent-care service now for an urgent assessment. Do not wait for another episode to prove something is wrong. Tell the service that you are pregnant and have vomited blood so they can direct you to the appropriate care.

Ordinary pregnancy sickness and bleeding are different

Nausea and vomiting can happen at any time of day. They often begin early in pregnancy and improve over time, but there is no guarantee that symptoms end at twelve or fourteen weeks. Most affected people improve by twenty weeks; some need help for longer.

Repeated vomiting that stops you eating, drinking or functioning can be hyperemesis gravidarum. It deserves treatment even without blood. New vomiting later in pregnancy, pain or other unusual symptoms also needs assessment for causes beyond pregnancy sickness. Being accustomed to nausea should not make a new bleeding symptom seem routine.

Blood can come from the mouth, nose or digestive tract

The medical term for vomiting blood is hematemesis. Blood may originate in the food pipe or stomach, or may have been swallowed from the mouth or nose before you vomit. The upper digestive tract also includes the first part of the small intestine, where ulcers can occur.

Fresh-looking red blood and darker material are both relevant. A dark or grainy appearance can develop when blood has been exposed to stomach contents; it is not proof that the problem has safely passed. Tell the clinician what you saw without trying to diagnose its origin yourself. A photograph can be useful if already available, but collecting one must not delay care.

Bleeding gums need dental attention

Pregnancy can make gum inflammation more noticeable. Red, tender or swollen gums may bleed with brushing or eating. Persistent bad breath, receding gums or increasing sensitivity are further reasons to arrange a dental examination. Blood from an irritated mouth may be swallowed and then appear when you are sick.

Mention any gum bleeding during the medical assessment, but do not assume it explains blood in vomit. For ongoing dental care, brush with fluoride toothpaste twice daily and clean between the teeth each day. These habits support gum health; they do not replace assessment of unexplained bleeding or treat a digestive-tract bleed.

A nosebleed can leave swallowed blood

Nosebleeds are more common during pregnancy. Sometimes blood travels down the back of the throat instead of being obvious at the nostrils, particularly if the head is tilted back. Swallowing it can make you feel sick or bring blood into vomit. Tell the team about a recent nosebleed, nasal congestion or blood noticed in your mouth.

For an active nosebleed, sit leaning forward and pinch the soft part of the nose continuously for ten to fifteen minutes, breathing through your mouth. Avoid tipping your head back to swallow the blood. Heavy or persistent bleeding, weakness, breathing trouble or swallowing enough blood to vomit needs urgent help. This possible explanation should not postpone assessment.

Retching can irritate tissue or cause a lining tear

Stomach acid and repeated retching can leave the mouth, throat or food pipe sore. A burning throat does not identify the source of bleeding, however. A clinician may need to check for inflammation, reflux-related damage or another injury.

A Mallory–Weiss tear is a split in the inner lining, usually near where the food pipe joins the stomach. Forceful vomiting or coughing can trigger it. Severe pregnancy vomiting, a hiatus hernia and eating disorders are among the relevant history to discuss. Such tears sometimes heal with supportive treatment, but they can also bleed significantly and may need an endoscopic procedure. Do not use the possibility of a small tear as reassurance to stay home.

A full-thickness rupture is a different emergency

Boerhaave syndrome means a tear through the whole wall of the food pipe. It can allow digestive contents to escape into the chest, causing serious infection. It is different from a superficial lining tear, even though both can follow violent vomiting.

Severe chest or upper abdominal pain after vomiting, breathlessness, fever or pain spreading to the back or neck requires emergency assessment. Do not wait for a large amount of blood or for every possible symptom to appear. The number of weeks pregnant does not provide a reliable way to rule this injury out.

Ulcers and inflammation are other possible causes

An ulcer is an open sore in the stomach or duodenal lining. Symptoms may include upper abdominal discomfort, bloating, belching, nausea or feeling full unusually quickly. Some ulcers cause few symptoms until bleeding occurs, so the absence of longstanding stomach pain is not reassuring.

The most common causes are Helicobacter pylori infection and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medicines such as ibuprofen or aspirin. Everyday emotional stress is not the usual explanation. Gastritis and inflammation of the food pipe are other possibilities. Mention previous ulcers, liver disease, a bleeding disorder or an earlier digestive bleed so the clinician can consider the full picture.

Report pregnancy symptoms separately as well

Blood in vomit is not, by itself, a diagnosis of miscarriage. It also cannot establish that the pregnancy is healthy. Your condition and any pregnancy symptoms need their own assessment; reassuring yourself from one symptom alone can miss a separate problem.

Tell the maternity team about vaginal bleeding, passing tissue, leaking fluid, strong abdominal or back pain, a severe headache or visual changes. Heavy vaginal bleeding, collapse or severe pain needs emergency care. These symptoms should not be folded into an assumption that everything comes from morning sickness. Explain clearly which blood came from vomiting and which came from the vagina, if both occurred.

What to tell the team and what they may check

Describe when the vomiting began, how many episodes occurred, the amount and appearance of blood, whether retching came first, and any pain, black stools, faintness or reduced urine. Bring your medication and supplement list, including prescribed aspirin, blood thinners and anti-sickness treatment. If you cannot remember quantities precisely, an honest estimate is more useful than delaying the call.

Assessment can include pulse, blood pressure, breathing, oxygen level, hydration and blood tests. An upper endoscopy uses a flexible camera to inspect the food pipe and stomach and can sometimes treat a bleeding site. Ultrasound, MRI, CT or X-rays are considered only when relevant to the suspected problem. The team weighs the need for each investigation during pregnancy; this is not a checklist that everyone must undergo.

Treatment is chosen for the cause and blood loss

The first priorities are to assess your stability and control significant bleeding. Treatment may involve intravenous fluids, anti-sickness medication, acid-reducing treatment, a blood transfusion or an endoscopic procedure. Some people need observation; others need more intensive treatment. A full-thickness rupture requires specialist hospital care and may need endoscopic repair or surgery.

An ulcer does not automatically mean antibiotics. If H. pylori is identified, the team decides which treatment is appropriate and when to use it during pregnancy. Ask what caused the bleeding, what treatment addresses it and what symptoms mean you should return. Relief of nausea alone does not establish that the bleeding source has healed.

Review medicines rather than self-treating

Do not add ibuprofen, aspirin or another anti-inflammatory painkiller for the discomfort. Tell the treating clinician immediately if you already take prescribed aspirin or an anticoagulant, and ask how to handle the next dose. A medicine may have an important pregnancy indication, so changing it without an individualized plan can create another risk.

Pregnancy-compatible treatments for nausea are available. Tell the team if tablets will not stay down or a prescription has stopped helping. Severe prolonged vomiting may require fluid and electrolyte treatment and thiamine, a vitamin given as part of supervised care. Supplements and nonprescription products belong on the medication list too.

Home nausea remedies come after assessment

Ginger may help some people with ordinary pregnancy nausea, but it does not treat bleeding. Concentrated products can cause heartburn or irritation and need a medication-interaction check. A ginger tea, sweet or capsule is not a reason to postpone medical help. No particular ginger dose should be started for blood in vomit.

Vitamin B6 is used in some nausea-treatment plans, sometimes with another medicine. The dose should account for other supplements you take. Peppermint, berry juices and other foods may suit individual tastes but are not established treatments for a bleeding episode. Once the team advises that eating and drinking are appropriate, follow the agreed recovery plan and discuss persistent nausea rather than repeatedly trying new remedies.

Recovery includes a clear return plan

Significant blood loss can lead to anemia or shock, and continued vomiting can worsen dehydration and poor intake. Reduced urination, increasing weakness, confusion, clammy skin or faintness should not be dismissed as ordinary pregnancy fatigue. Prompt treatment supports both your health and the pregnancy, without a guarantee about outcomes from the symptom alone.

Before leaving care, check who to contact if blood returns, how to take the prescribed medicines and whether follow-up blood tests or specialist appointments are needed. Ask someone you trust for practical help while you recover. A recurrence needs reassessment even if an earlier episode settled or a previous cause seemed minor.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

NHS guidance calls for medical help for vomiting blood.

NIDDK describes cause-directed assessment and treatment, while RCOG explains care for severe pregnancy sickness. These are related but distinct problems.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to keep questions and recovery notes together after seeking care. A saved symptom entry does not notify an emergency service.

When to seek help

Blood in vomit with feeling unwell, faintness, abdominal pain, black stools or breathing difficulty needs emergency assessment. If it has stopped without other symptoms, seek urgent medical advice now.

Evidence notes updated: October 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Blood in vomit is not routine morning sickness, even if the amount seems small.
  • Gum or nose bleeding, lining injuries and ulcers are possible causes; assessment identifies the source.
  • A superficial lining tear and a full-thickness food-pipe rupture are different injuries.
  • Medication, investigations and treatment depend on the cause and your condition.
  • Nausea remedies must not delay urgent assessment, and recurrent bleeding needs another call.

Frequently asked questions

Can a small streak of blood be ignored?

No. Contact your maternity or urgent-care service promptly even if it has stopped. Other symptoms or ongoing bleeding can make this an emergency.

Is coffee-ground vomit safer than red blood?

No. Dark or grainy material may be altered blood and still needs assessment.

Could a nosebleed explain it?

Swallowed blood can appear in vomit, but tell a clinician rather than assuming that is the only cause.

Should I stop brushing if my gums bleed?

Arrange a dental assessment and continue gentle fluoride brushing and daily cleaning between the teeth. Dental care does not replace medical advice for vomiting blood.

Can retching cause a tear?

Yes. A lining tear can follow repeated retching, and a much rarer full-thickness rupture is a separate emergency. You cannot distinguish them reliably at home.

Does vomiting blood mean a miscarriage?

Not by itself. Report vaginal bleeding, pain or leaking fluid separately; neither pregnancy wellbeing nor pregnancy loss can be determined from vomiting blood alone.

Will everyone need an endoscopy or scan?

No. The clinician selects investigations according to the bleeding, suspected cause and pregnancy.

Should I stop prescribed aspirin myself?

Tell the treating clinician about it immediately and ask for instructions about the next dose. Do not independently change an important prescription or take extra doses for pain.

Can ginger or vitamin B6 treat the bleeding?

No. They may be considered for nausea in an appropriate plan, but bleeding requires its own assessment and treatment.

What if the blood comes back after treatment?

Seek reassessment and follow the return instructions. Use emergency care if bleeding continues or you feel unwell, faint, breathless or have significant pain.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
